There are also other constructor variants to cover, like ReadableInstant with ReadableDuration, a plain long duration, and the Object-based period constructor, plus a long list of protected methods like setField, mergePeriod, addPeriod, and setValues that need exposing through a subclass since they live in the base package.

Now I'm planning test cases to cover, starting with the constructor that takes 8 ints plus a PeriodType, checking normal cases against standard and year-month-day-time types.

I need tests for unsupported field values: passing a non-zero weeks value with yearMonthDay() type should throw IllegalArgumentException, while passing zero for an unsupported field should pass without error since checkAndUpdate treats index==-1 with newValue==0 as fine.

Next I'm thinking through the constructor that takes start/end longs plus a type.

Then the constructor variants with ReadableInstant pairs - testing nulls defaulting to zero values with the type still set, and testing actual non-null instants too.

For the ReadablePartial constructor, I'm planning tests for null inputs throwing exceptions, same-class partials like LocalDate taking a fast path, and mismatched sizes or field types triggering exceptions. Non-contiguous partials are tricky to construct, so I may need to use the Partial class specifically for the mismatched field types case since it's not a BaseLocal subclass.

For the duration-based constructors, I'll test null instant/duration combos defaulting to now and zero respectively, plus the single-long-duration constructor delegating with a standard type.

I should also test the type-and-chronology constructor with an explicit period type, and the object-based constructor by passing a Period instance that goes through the converter manager.

For the ReadWritablePeriod branch, since my TestPeriod subclass doesn't implement that interface it falls into the else path using MutablePeriod, so I need to create a second test class that actually implements ReadWritablePeriod to exercise that branch properly.

Implementing the full interface would require public setValue/setField/add methods beyond what BasePeriod already provides, which adds significant complexity given my time budget — I'll skip covering that specific branch and note the gap instead.

Moving on to the simpler constructor that takes an int array and period type, then the core accessor methods: checkPeriodType delegates to DateTimeUtils.getPeriodType, getPeriodType returns the stored type, size delegates to the type's size, getFieldType returns the field type at an index with bounds checking, and getValue returns the value at an index, also needing bounds checks against IndexOutOfBoundsException.

For the duration conversions, I'm thinking through toDurationFrom and toDurationTo with both explicit and null instants. Then for mutation, setPeriod needs testing both with a ReadablePeriod (null defaults to zeros, valid periods match values, unsupported non-zero fields throw IllegalArgumentException) and with the eight-int overload, plus setField/setFieldInto behavior for supported fields at valid indices.

I also need to cover setField/setFieldInto when the field is unsupported with nonzero value (throws) and when field is null, which should throw regardless of value since the null check triggers independently. For addField/addFieldInto, the logic mirrors this but uses safeAdd when supported, and I could consider testing overflow behavior though that's really FieldUtils' concern rather than the core class. Next I want to test mergePeriod and mergePeriodInto similarly.

Negative values should pass through fine since there's no sign validation, only support validation. I'll structure the actual test methods with assertions using PeriodType.standard(), yearMonthDay(), dayTime(), etc., and use org.joda.time.Period as a convenient ReadablePeriod implementation for the setPeriod/mergePeriod/addPeriod tests.

For the object converter test, I'll use an existing Period instance as the safer source object rather than relying on String-to-Period conversion support, since ReadablePeriodConverter is reliably registered. I should also add an overflow-safety test checking that adding Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 triggers an ArithmeticException via safeAdd.

For the constructor(2) test with start/end millis, I'll use ISOChronology.getInstanceUTC() to avoid timezone ambiguity, picking a fixed start instant (epoch zero) and a fixed end instant so expected field values can be computed precisely rather than asserting loosely.

Since a single day is shorter than a week, the algorithm leaves it as days=1 with weeks=0, so the expected period has days at index 3 (after years, months, weeks) equal to 1. I'll check the size is 8 and that specific index matches rather than asserting every field.

For the instant-pair and partial constructors, I'm planning similar tests: null/null should zero out all fields, while actual DateTime or LocalDate pairs one day apart should also yield days=1 under the standard period type, verifying the chronology correctly computes the difference.

I also want to test mismatched partial types, like LocalDate versus LocalTime, which have different field sizes and should throw an IllegalArgumentException since they can't share a fast path or match sizes.

For same-size mismatches, I can construct two Partial instances sharing a year field but differing in the second field type (month versus day), which should trigger the "same set of fields" exception since the field types don't align positionally.

I should also add tests for null start/end arguments expecting exceptions, and possibly skip the contiguous test case if it's too complex to set up cleanly.

For the other constructors taking ReadableInstant/ReadableDuration combinations, I'll use a fixed UTC DateTime at epoch and a one-day Duration to get deterministic results, testing both the (instant, duration, type) and (duration, instant, type) orderings and verifying the computed start/end millis align correctly.

For null defaults I just verify no exception is thrown since exact values depend on "now". For the simpler long-duration constructors, I'll test with a 1-hour millisecond duration under standard PeriodType with ISO chronology, confirming only precise fields (hours, minutes, seconds, millis) get populated since years/months/weeks aren't precise in that context.

So even with DST, days become imprecise but hours remain fixed at exactly 3600000ms, making hours=1 the safe expectation regardless of the test environment's default zone. For the explicit chronology case, I'll try a similar deterministic setup using UTC with standard period type to avoid any zone ambiguity.

For the second explicit example, I'll use ISOChronology.getInstanceUTC() with dayTime period type since UTC has no DST and days become precise there — 90000000ms works out to exactly 1 day and 1 hour, so I expect days=1, hours=1, and everything else zero.

This is getting complicated, so I'll simplify: just verify no exceptions are thrown and check basic correctness for the clean 1-hour default case and the explicit UTC day-precision case, rather than exhaustively testing every combination. Then I'll move on to testing the object-based constructor using an existing Period instance.

I'm constructing a source Period with all fields set (years through millis) using the standard type, then building a TestPeriod from it with null type and chrono to verify it inherits the source's period type and matching values. Next I want to test passing an explicit incompatible type like yearMonthDay against a source period that has nonzero weeks, to see whether it throws an IllegalArgumentException due to field support mismatch.

Good, that covers a useful branch worth testing. I should also check boundary conditions for getValue/getFieldType at index 0, the last index, and invalid indices like -1 or size (expecting IndexOutOfBoundsException), confirm getPeriodType() returns the expected type, and then move to testing toDurationFrom/toDurationTo using a TestPeriod built directly from an int array and a DateTime start point at epoch.

I expect converting that one-day period to a duration from the start instant gives exactly 86400000 milliseconds, and I'll mirror that for toDurationTo with an end instant. For the null-instant case where "now" is used internally, I'll just verify no exception is thrown and that a Duration object comes back, without checking an exact value since "now" isn't deterministic.

Now I'll write out these as proper @Test methods, double-checking I'm using the correct Joda-Time imports and APIs matching the older 2.0-era library version this bug corresponds to.

I also want a test where setField is called with a null field to confirm the index==-1 && field==null branch throws, tracing through how setFieldInto and indexOf would handle a null comparison.

Since indexOf with a null type returns -1 safely (reference equality just fails to match), the condition correctly throws an IllegalArgumentException regardless of value, so that path is safe to test directly.
